You are developing an automated evaluation benchmark suite for a multiturn enterprise support agent that interacts with dynamic backend tools. In your current CI/CD pipeline, static golden datasets frequently produce failure signals because live backend dependencies return state that changes over time, while the current evaluation prompts do not assess tool-trajectory correctness, ambiguous user inputs, or API fault conditions. You need to ensure evaluation fidelity, ambiguity handling, and environment resilience.

What should you do?
explanation: Simulated tool responses decouple benchmark runs from changing backend state, making results more repeatable. Evaluation cases can cover ambiguous requests and simulated API errors, while trajectory metrics check the agent’s tool calls as well as its final responses. Those cases and metrics must be explicitly configured; mocking alone does not provide that coverage. ([docs.cloud.google.com](https://docs.cloud.google.com/gemini-enterprise-agent-platform/optimize/evaluation/agent-evaluation))

options.A: Use static simulated tool responses to decouple evaluation from dynamic backend state changes, and construct test sets in the gen AI evaluation service.
options.B: Run trigger-based CI/CD pipelines, and trigger Cloud Monitoring alerts when LLM-as-a-judge response evaluation metrics fall below baseline thresholds during live tool calls.
options.C: Replace the trigger-based CI/CD evaluation pipeline with an online LLM-as-a-judge mechanism that evaluates the live agent’s trajectory and outputs in production using continuous monitoring.
options.D: Deploy automated human-in-the-loop review tasks using Agent Designer to evaluate expected outputs when backend API dependencies return variable tool states.

question:
You manage a support agent that uses RAG to answer questions based on a document corpus in RAG Engine. Each query retrieves the top 50 chunks. While reviewing a set of failing questions, you determine that the chunk containing the answer is among the 50 returned but is ranked near the bottom, and the agent answers from a higher-ranked chunk instead.

You want to improve the answering chunk’s relevance ranking without re-indexing the corpus. The retrieval step has 200 milliseconds of headroom.

What should you do?
explanation: The Agent Platform ranking API reranks retrieved chunks by their relevance to the query, so it can promote an answer-bearing chunk without re-indexing the corpus. Google describes the reranker as having latency of less than 100 milliseconds, making it suitable for the available 200-millisecond headroom. Reranking improves relevance but does not guarantee that the correct chunk will always rank first. ([docs.cloud.google.com](https://docs.cloud.google.com/gemini-enterprise-agent-platform/build/rag-engine/retrieval-and-ranking))

options.A: Update the RAG Engine deployment configuration from the Spanner mode Basic tier to the Scaled tier.
options.B: Add the Agent Platform ranking API as the Agent Search reranker to reorder the chunks.
options.C: Set a vector_distance_threshold on the RAG Engine retrieval configuration to return more relevant chunks.
options.D: Add a reranker that calls a Gemini model to score each retrieved chunk, and reorder the chunks based on the user’s input.

question:
You are evaluating a policy question-answering agent with an Agent Development Kit (ADK) eval set. Each case stores one reference answer, and the ADK eval suite scores responses using the ADK `response_match_score` criterion. Reviewers have been asked to evaluate the agent’s responses and identify acceptable responses that cite the policy section and provide any exception applicable to the prompt. However, reviewers cannot agree on which answer to store because several substantially different answers are acceptable.

You want ADK evaluations to score responses against those two explicit semantic criteria instead of similarity to a single reference answer, with judge verdicts validated by reviewers.

What should you do?
explanation: Define rubrics for citing the policy section and providing any applicable exception, and use `rubric_based_final_response_quality_v1` to evaluate responses against them without relying on one reference answer. Set the combined-score threshold to 1.0 to require both rubrics to pass. The criterion uses an LLM judge, so its verdicts are not guaranteed to be error-free. ([github.com](https://github.com/google/adk-docs/blob/main/docs/evaluate/criteria.md))

options.A: Store several reference answers in each ADK eval case.
options.B: Lower the response_match_score threshold that the ADK eval set requires to pass.
options.C: Score the cases using the ADK final_response_match_v2 criterion against the stored reference answer.
options.D: Define evaluation rubrics, and score the responses using the ADK rubric_based_final_response_quality_v1 criterion.

question:
You are building a custom customer service agent and have compiled a golden dataset of historical user questions, reference documents, ideal answers and captured retrieval/tool traces. Before deploying the agent, you need to programmatically evaluate both the relevance of retrieved documents and the groundedness of the agent’s generated responses. You want to minimize custom evaluation code.

What should you do?
explanation: ADK evaluation tooling can run the agent against a golden dataset and use LLM-based autoraters to assess its behavior before deployment. Configured criteria can assess retrieved-document relevance, while grounding or hallucination metrics can check whether responses are supported by retrieved context. The evaluation must capture that context or the relevant tool traces; ideal answers alone are not sufficient. BLEU and ROUGE measure textual overlap rather than these RAG-specific properties. ([google.github.io](https://google.github.io/agents-cli/guide/evaluation/))

options.A: Deploy the agent to Agent Runtime, run the agent against the golden dataset, and review the metrics using Google Cloud Observability.
options.B: Run ADK evaluation tooling with compatible custom rubrics/autoraters that inspect retrieved context and generated answers against the reference evidence.
options.C: Configure a continuous evaluation pipeline using the Agent Search ranking API to compare the semantic similarity between the agent’s generated response and the golden dataset’s ideal answer.
options.D: Run a batch evaluation job against the agent using the golden dataset to calculate BLEU and ROUGE scores for the generated responses.

question: You are prototyping human-in-the-loop controls for a TypeScript ADK agent. Sensitive tool calls must be intercepted before execution, and an authenticated reviewer must approve the exact pending call through a trusted UI. The evaluation keeps the same live runner/session available while waiting; restart durability is outside this prototype. Which documented policy-based pattern should you use?
explanation: The TypeScript SecurityPlugin consults a policy engine and requests confirmation before sensitive tool execution. The application must authenticate the approver and bind the response to the pending call. This prototype does not assume managed-session or restart persistence. ([ADK policy pattern](https://github.com/google/adk-docs/blob/main/docs/workflows/patterns.md))

options.A: Attach SecurityPlugin with a BasePolicyEngine that returns PolicyOutcome.CONFIRM, keep the live runner/session available, and return the authenticated reviewer’s decision through the matching confirmation FunctionResponse.
options.B: Configure Agent Gateway using GatewayPolicyInterceptor to intercept tool payloads, log execution traces using CloudLoggingService, and allow the agent model to parse user natural language confirmation responses from the chat stream.
options.C: Configure event notifications using PubSubEventBridge, persist pending execution state using a custom GcsStateStore, and deploy a Cloud Run function that evaluates user approvals using an LLM classification prompt to update the confirmation flag.
options.D: Configure Model Armor security templates using FilterConfig to detect sensitive tool requests, pause agent containers using ContainerLifecycleManager, and resume execution when a user submits a natural language approval prompt.

question: A managed credential integration already obtains and refreshes short-lived Google OAuth access tokens for the authorized calling principal. Your agent must call a data agent through the Conversational Analytics API in another project. Which HTTP authentication header and baseline data-agent role should the integration use? Additional source-data permissions are handled separately.
explanation: Use Authorization: Bearer with the short-lived Google OAuth access token. The dataAgentUser role supports chatting with the target data agent; underlying source access still needs its own permissions. Header formatting alone is not a credential-refresh implementation. ([Conversational Analytics authentication](https://docs.cloud.google.com/gemini/data-agents/conversational-analytics-api/build-agent-http))

options.A: - Generate a long-lived service account key in the downstream project, and pass the service account key JSON in the request payload. 2. Grant the service account the roles/geminidataanalytics.dataAgentCreator IAM role hosting the Conversational Analytics API.
options.B: - Configure the tool execution calls to pass an OIDC Identity Token in a custom X-Goog-IAP-JWT-Assertion header. 2. Grant the calling principal the roles/geminidataanalytics.dataAgentViewer IAM role on the downstream project hosting the Conversational Analytics API.
options.C: - Configure the tool execution calls to pass a standard Google OAuth 2.0 bearer token in the HTTP Authorization header. 2. Grant the calling principal the roles/geminidataanalytics.dataAgentUser IAM role on the downstream project hosting the Conversational Analytics API.
options.D: - Implement tool execution calls to pass a signed OAuth 2.0 refresh token as an HTTP query parameter. 2. Grant the calling principal the roles/geminidataanalytics.queryDataUser IAM role on the downstream project hosting the Conversational Analytics API.

question:
You are deploying an autonomous coding agent on Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) to run user-requested Python scripts. To isolate untrusted code execution, you enabled GKE Agent Sandbox with gVisor to intercept container system calls in user space. During a security audit, you find that an untrusted Python script generated by a prompt injection attack successfully fetched IAM identity tokens by sending an HTTP request to the link-local instance metadata server at 169.254.169.254.

You need to prevent sandboxed code from exfiltrating metadata tokens while maintaining container kernel isolation.

What should you do?
explanation: An egress NetworkPolicy can prevent the sandbox Pod from initiating requests to the metadata server while gVisor continues to provide kernel isolation. Configure the policy so that no applicable egress rule permits metadata access; the effective metadata address depends on the GKE dataplane. ([docs.cloud.google.com](https://docs.cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/concepts/sandbox-pods))

options.A: Apply domain restrictions to the sandbox Pod.
options.B: Apply an enforced egress NetworkPolicy allowlist to the sandbox Pod that excludes the observed metadata endpoint and other unapproved metadata paths; retain gVisor kernel isolation.
options.C: Apply a Kubernetes NetworkPolicy to the sandbox Pod that blocks ingress traffic to 169.254.169.254.
options.D: Reconfigure the gVisor Sentry process to disable the execve system call for child Python processes.

question:
You are designing an enterprise multiagent procurement system in Google Cloud. An orchestrator agent processes vendor purchase orders, retrieves contract terms, and invokes downstream tools. Vendor document text reaches the gateway through supported tool-response payloads. Your organization requires inspection to reduce prompt-injection risk, and high-risk financial actions must receive explicit compliance officer authorization before execution.

How should you meet these requirements?
explanation:
Model Armor security templates on Agent Gateway can inspect supported agent and tool traffic for prompt injection, including malicious instructions in retrieved content. Human-in-the-loop approval controls can pause high-risk financial tool calls until a compliance officer authorizes them, before execution. ([docs.cloud.google.com](https://docs.cloud.google.com/architecture/multiagent-ai-system))

Gateway integration does not screen document or file uploads such as PDFs directly; those require direct Model Armor document screening. ([docs.cloud.google.com](https://docs.cloud.google.com/gemini-enterprise-agent-platform/govern/configure-model-armor))

options.A: Configure Model Armor baseline harm category filters in Model Garden, and implement prompt rules directing the model to ignore embedded commands.
options.B: Configure Model Armor post-execution log sink filters in Cloud Logging, and implement a Cloud Run functions webhook to notify compliance officers after transaction completion.
options.C: Configure Model Armor security templates on downstream tool invocation outputs, and implement an asynchronous Workflows execution logic with a human-approval step using a persistent database.
options.D: Configure Model Armor security templates at Agent Gateway for dynamic payload inspection, and implement human-in-the-loop approval policies on tools.

question:
You are designing a secure, multiagent framework on Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform. An administrative assistant agent needs access to internal corporate wikis and external communication APIs to synthesize daily updates and draft emails.

You need to establish a security architecture integrated with Agent Gateway to protect against indirect prompt injections and data exfiltration. You want the framework to scan user input prompts and retrieved message content in real time, while enforcing an explicit authorization boundary for critical, state-modifying operations.

What should you do?
explanation: Model Armor templates integrated with Agent Gateway can screen user prompts and supported tool requests and responses for prompt injection and sensitive data leakage. A human-in-the-loop checkpoint can require explicit approval before a critical state-modifying API operation proceeds. Screening depends on the payload types supported by the gateway integration. ([docs.cloud.google.com](https://docs.cloud.google.com/gemini-enterprise-agent-platform/govern/configure-model-armor))

options.A: Configure Model Armor templates to scan ingress prompts and egress responses, and implement human-in-the-loop approval policies for mutating API execution flows.
options.B: Configure Model Armor to perform network-level packet filtering and IP address blocking at the Agent Gateway ingress subnet, and schedule daily offline Model Armor batch jobs to sanitize prompt histories stored in backend databases.
options.C: Create VPC Service Controls perimeter configurations around the Agent Gateway, and apply IAM Conditions to restrict backend API access permissions based on temporal context.
options.D: Configure Model Armor templates on the Agent Gateway to scan ingress prompts only, and assign resource-level IAM roles to authorize downstream API tool executions.

question:
You are building a customer support agent. To meet corporate governance policies, you must apply centrally enforced screening/redaction of configured PII types before supported responses reach users, and validate the detector’s coverage. You want to enforce these guardrails without changing the agent’s core app code.

How should you configure this governance?
explanation: Model Armor can use Sensitive Data Protection to detect configured types of sensitive information in agent responses. Applied through Agent Gateway with enforcement enabled, it can block or redact detected violations without adding filtering logic to the agent’s core code. For redaction, configure advanced Sensitive Data Protection settings with a de-identification template and use `INSPECT_AND_BLOCK`. Detection is not a guarantee that every possible PII instance will be identified. ([docs.cloud.google.com](https://docs.cloud.google.com/gemini-enterprise-agent-platform/govern/configure-model-armor))

options.A: Configure an Agent Gateway routing rule to intercept traffic and route the traffic through a custom Cloud Run webhook that performs regex string matching for PII.
options.B: Deploy the agent within a VPC Service Controls perimeter, and configure an egress rule that drops HTTP responses containing PII payloads.
options.C: Configure a Model Armor template with advanced Sensitive Data Protection settings and a de-identification template, and enforce it through Agent Gateway using INSPECT_AND_BLOCK.
options.D: Update the agent’s system prompt with strict negative instructions forbidding the generation of PII.

question:
You are designing the enterprise governance and observability layer for a distributed multiagent deployment in Google Cloud. You want autonomous subagents to communicate across microservices and external capability servers using agentic communication protocols. You need a solution that meets the following compliance controls:

- Provide unified visibility to catalog active agent instances.

- Capture protocol interaction payloads for compliance auditing.

- Monitor interagent communication traffic without requiring code modifications to individual agent services.

How should you design the solution?
explanation: Gateway request metadata alone does not meet a full-body audit requirement. Use the documented service-extension integration for supported request/response body capture and validate redaction, access and retention separately. ([Apigee extension for Agent Gateway](https://docs.cloud.google.com/apigee/docs/api-platform/service-extensions/extension-processor-agent-gateway))

options.A: Use Agent Gateway with Agent Registry for centralized discovery and traffic governance, and configure a supported Apigee service extension/body-logging integration for the required audited payloads with appropriate redaction and access controls.
options.B: Deploy Agent Gateway as an egress-only web proxy to inspect outbound internet endpoints and validate external domain service queries.
options.C: Deploy Apigee API Gateway with message logging policies to manage agent endpoints and capture outbound API payload traffic.
options.D: Configure Cloud Service Mesh with egress-only L7 policies to inspect outbound internet endpoints and validate external domain service queries for authorized agent traffic.

question:
You are deploying an enterprise conversational agent in Google Cloud that connects to sensitive human resources (HR) databases. Your organization’s compliance policy requires all user queries and model completions to be filtered in real time to prevent prompt injection attacks, block harmful content, and sanitize personally identifiable information (PII) before responses reach the user interface. You need to implement a managed security enforcement layer that meets these requirements with minimal latency.

What should you do?
explanation: Agent Gateway can centrally apply Model Armor filters to supported client requests and agent responses, blocking prompt injection and harmful content. Advanced Sensitive Data Protection settings link inspection and de-identification templates to sanitize matching PII. Configure the Model Armor template with INSPECT_AND_BLOCK enforcement: PII-only violations are redacted, while payloads that also violate other detectors are blocked. Gateway coverage depends on the traffic and methods supported by the integration. ([docs.cloud.google.com](https://docs.cloud.google.com/gemini-enterprise-agent-platform/govern/configure-model-armor))

options.A: Apply a Sensitive Data Protection de-identification template at the Agent Gateway, and filter for injection and harmful content using Model Armor’s input and output templates
options.B: Enforce Model Armor filter templates with linked Sensitive Data Protection de-identification templates at the Agent Gateway for all agent traffic.
options.C: Deploy a custom Llama Guard model on Model Garden behind the Agent Gateway, and add a Sensitive Data Protection inspection template for PII.
options.D: Configure Model Armor filter templates with linked Sensitive Data Protection de-identification templates, and attach them to each agent’s runtime.

question:
You are implementing an agent built with Agent Development Kit (ADK) and deployed in Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE). The agent automatically generates and runs Python data analysis scripts based on user-provided datasets. You want to ensure that the AI-generated code runs safely, preventing potentially malicious code from accessing the internet, exfiltrating data, or reading the host system’s environment variables.

You need to implement a deterministic, infrastructure-level boundary specifically for the code execution phase without breaking the agent’s primary reasoning loop.

What should you do?
explanation: A sandbox provides an infrastructure boundary for generated code while allowing the ADK agent to continue its reasoning loop and receive execution results. Configure the sandbox to deny internet egress and keep host environment variables and credentials inaccessible. Sandbox defaults must be checked: for example, Agent Sandbox on GKE allows public internet egress by default. ([google.github.io](https://google.github.io/adk-docs/tools/google-cloud/code-exec-agent-engine/))

options.A: Update the agent’s system prompt with explicit system instructions forbidding the LLM from generating code that imports external network libraries or reads local variables.
options.B: Wrap the agent’s deployment in a VPC Service Controls perimeter, and configure an egress rule that drops all outbound internet traffic from the agent’s service account.
options.C: Route generated scripts to a supported isolated execution sandbox configured without host credentials/environment mounts and with internet egress denied, while the primary agent receives only the execution results.
options.D: Configure a Model Armor policy with a custom Sensitive Data Protection dictionary to scan and block any Python network or OS library imports in the agent’s generated code.

question:
You are deploying an agent on Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform in Project-A, a dedicated runtime Google Cloud project. The agent needs to retrieve database API credentials from Secret Manager in Project-B, a centralized governance project, and query an Agent Search data store also hosted in Project-B. You are using Agent Identity to govern the agent’s permissions across projects. You need to grant the minimum required cross-project IAM access while following the principle of least privilege.

What should you do?
explanation: Grant the agent identity Secret Manager Secret Accessor on the specific secret containing the database API credentials, and Discovery Engine Viewer on the target data store. The former permits access to the secret payload; the latter includes search permission without granting editor access. ([docs.cloud.google.com](https://docs.cloud.google.com/secret-manager/docs/access-control))

options.A: Grant the roles/secretmanager.user IAM role to the agent’s identity at the Project-B project level.
options.B: Grant roles/secretmanager.secretAccessor to the agent identity on the specific Secret Manager secret containing the database credentials in Project-B.
options.C: Grant the roles/discoveryengine.editor IAM role to Project-A’s agent identity at the Project-B project level.
options.D: Grant the roles/discoveryengine.viewer IAM role to the agent’s identity scoped to the target Agent Search data store resource in Project-B.
options.E: Grant the roles/iam.serviceAccountTokenCreator IAM role to Project-B’s agent identity to allow cross-project impersonation.

question:
You are designing an enterprise agentic platform that connects autonomous agents to internal managed databases, custom API endpoints, and third-party software-as-a-service (SaaS) integrations. Individual product teams build redundant integration adapters and connect to remote services, resulting in fragmented security boundaries and high maintenance overhead. You need to implement a unified architecture to standardize these integrations securely.

What should you do?
explanation: MCP servers provide reusable, standardized access to data and APIs. Agent Registry Service resources can register custom endpoints for centralized discovery and governance. IAM policies control access, while Model Armor floor settings provide complementary content screening—not authorization—for supported integrations. Automatic MCP floor-setting enforcement should not be assumed to cover every custom server. ([docs.cloud.google.com](https://docs.cloud.google.com/agent-registry/register-mcp-servers))

options.A: Deploy MCP servers for data and API access.Register API endpoints in Cloud API Gateway using OpenAPI specifications.Enforce VPC Service Controls perimeters.
options.B: Deploy MCP servers hosted alongside each agent instance.Store the configuration manifests in Artifact Registry.Grant the Service Account User IAM role to the agent identities.
options.C: Deploy MCP servers for each external service.Index the endpoints in Agent Search data stores for dynamic agent discovery.Manage tool access using the Restrict Resource Service Usage constraint.
options.D: Expose data/API capabilities through MCP servers, register custom endpoints as Agent Registry Service resources, enforce authorization with IAM, and apply supported Model Armor screening separately.

question: A healthcare organization has separately reviewed its contractual and regulatory requirements. Its technical policy requires approved processing locations, restricted private connectivity, customer-managed encryption for all in-scope persisted resources and a model validated for tool calling. Which TWO deployment patterns could satisfy these technical controls when the selected services/model versions explicitly support them? Neither pattern alone certifies legal compliance.
explanation: Both patterns require validation of the chosen model, service features, locations and every persisted-data path. PSC alone is not an air gap; private networking does not establish residency or encrypt every resource with a customer-managed key. ([Private access](https://docs.cloud.google.com/vpc/docs/private-access-options), [GKE CMEK](https://docs.cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/how-to/using-cmek))

options.A: Self-host a fine-tuned open-weights model on Cloud Run using default private endpoints with IAM user authentication.
options.B: Deploy a self-hosted LLM through a HTTP webhook using public internet routing and TLS 1.3 encryption.
options.C: Use the private Gemini API with standard API keys and rely on client-side prompt obfuscation to anonymize patient health records.
options.D: Choose a managed Gemini deployment documented to support the required private API connectivity, approved locations and customer-managed encryption for every in-scope resource, with access and data flows restricted accordingly.
options.E: Self-host a verified tool-capable Gemma variant with vLLM on private GKE infrastructure in approved locations, configure the required CMEK-backed resources and explicitly restrict egress and data flows.

question:
You are setting up a custom agent in Gemini Enterprise that uses a dedicated service account to query an Agent Search data store. During testing, grounded search queries fail with a 403 Permission Denied error indicating that the principal lacks the `discoveryengine.servingConfigs.search` permission on the data store resource. You need to fix this permission error while following the principle of least privilege.

What should you do?
explanation: The Discovery Engine Viewer role includes `discoveryengine.servingConfigs.search` and can be granted directly on a data store, limiting the grant to the resource the agent needs. It avoids the write or administrative access of broader roles; Cloud Storage object access does not provide the missing Discovery Engine permission. ([docs.cloud.google.com](https://docs.cloud.google.com/iam/docs/roles-permissions/discoveryengine))

options.A: Grant the roles/discoveryengine.editor IAM role to the agent’s service account on the Google Cloud project hosting the data store.
options.B: Grant the roles/discoveryengine.agentspaceAdmin IAM role to the agent’s service account on the target Gemini Enterprise app.
options.C: Grant the roles/discoveryengine.viewer IAM role to the agent’s service account on the data store resource.
options.D: Grant the roles/storage.objectViewer IAM role to the agent’s service account on a Cloud Storage bucket containing the original source documents.

question:
You are configuring a secure agent-to-tool API integration for a financial agent on Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform. The agent calls an internal payment processing microservice protected by OAuth 2.0.

To comply with strict enterprise security policy, you must ensure that:

- OAuth client credentials used for service-to-service tool authentication are encrypted at rest and never hardcoded in tool definitions or repository source code.

- Tool execution is strictly limited to the minimum required API permissions, so the agent cannot perform unauthorized administrative operations on the payment microservice.

What should you do?
explanation: Use a managed OAuth provider for client credentials and restrict/enforce the issued scopes. Provision credentials securely using the supported provider schema; a Secret Manager resource URI is not assumed to be an accepted client-secret field. ([2-legged OAuth](https://docs.cloud.google.com/iam/docs/auth-with-2lo-v2))

options.A: Grant the roles/owner IAM role on the payment microservice project to the agent’s identity.
options.B: Configure only the OAuth scopes required by the payment tool, associate the auth provider with that tool, and ensure the authorization server and payment service enforce those scopes.
options.C: Encode the OAuth client secret in Base64, and pass the secret in the tools.py environment variable map.
options.D: Configure the tool definition to use OAUTH2_IMPLICIT_GRANT with wildcard scopes (*).
options.E: Provision the OAuth client credentials securely into the Agent Identity auth manager’s managed 2-legged OAuth provider/vault, keeping them out of tool source and repository configuration.

question:
You are configuring enterprise agents that must dynamically discover and invoke capabilities across managed databases, third-party SaaS tools, and Google Cloud services. Your architecture hosts custom MCP servers on Cloud Run alongside pre-built Google Cloud MCP servers. Your operations team requires a centralized catalog to govern access controls, register JSON tool specifications, and manage IAM identities across all remote HTTP transport endpoints.

You need to maximize operational efficiency and maintain strict governance by establishing a single point of discovery and access control for both native and custom agent capabilities.

What should you do?
explanation:
Agent Registry provides a centralized catalog for MCP servers and their tools. Custom servers can be registered as Service resources with JSON tool specifications, while supported Google Cloud MCP servers are automatically registered when their APIs are enabled. ([docs.cloud.google.com](https://docs.cloud.google.com/agent-registry/register-mcp-servers))

Access to the actual endpoints must also be enforced through the appropriate authentication and authorization controls. For example, Cloud Run IAM can restrict invocation of a custom MCP server to authorized agent identities. ([docs.cloud.google.com](https://docs.cloud.google.com/run/docs/ai/authenticate-agents))

options.A: Register custom Cloud Run MCP servers as Service resources within Agent Registry, upload their JSON tool specifications, and enable built-in Google Cloud MCP servers to centralize agent capability discovery and IAM access governance.
options.B: Store local client configuration files containing remote HTTP endpoints in Secret Manager, and mount them across agent execution environments to handle tool discovery and endpoint authentication.
options.C: Deploy OpenAPI specifications for custom Cloud Run MCP servers using Cloud Endpoints, and register these endpoints in Service Directory to enable dynamic agent service discovery and endpoint-level IAM security.
options.D: Configure custom MCP servers on Cloud Run, and grant granular IAM roles to extension service accounts to manage agent access controls within defined VPC Service Controls perimeters.

question: You are evaluating an ADK payment-tool prototype in a controlled environment. Calls above a threshold must pause for an authenticated officer’s approval before execution. The same live runner and supported in-memory session remain available while the decision is pending; crash recovery is not part of this evaluation. Which approach uses the native tool-confirmation flow with the least additional infrastructure?
explanation: Native tool confirmation can pause a sensitive call and accept a matching FunctionResponse from the trusted application. Authenticate the approver separately. Current documentation lists DatabaseSessionService and VertexAiSessionService as unsupported, so do not infer durable managed-session support from this prototype. ([ADK confirmation](https://adk.dev/tools-custom/confirmation/))

options.A: Configure Cloud Tasks queues with rate limiting to delay tool calls, and execute Cloud Run functions to poll a database for approval status.
options.B: Configure conditional ADK tool confirmation, present the pending call in a trusted approval UI, and return the authorized decision with the matching confirmation call ID while retaining the live session.
options.C: Configure a Cloud Run function as an execution wrapper around all banking tools, and implement an approval tracking database.
options.D: Configure Pub/Sub message topics to buffer transaction payloads, and deploy Cloud Run functions to process approval tokens.

question:
You are deploying a custom Antigravity CLI plugin to enforce enterprise data loss prevention compliance across developer workstations. You must configure an event hook that intercepts tool calls immediately before file execution, automatically redacts sensitive API keys from generated code diffs in transit, and stops tool execution if sanitization fails.

What should you do?
explanation: A command PreToolUse hook receives the proposed toolCall and can return a gating decision plus overwrite arguments. Sanitization failure must produce deny; an unhandled process error must not be assumed to block. Inspect/Decide/Transform are not documented hook types. ([Antigravity hooks](https://antigravity.google/docs/hooks))

options.A: Configure a command PreToolUse hook whose wrapper validates/sanitizes proposed arguments and emits allow with overwrite only on success; emit deny on a handled sanitization failure, and verify timeout/crash handling is fail-closed.
options.B: Define a Decide hook in a hooks.json file bound to the pre-tool execution event, and implement a handler function that evaluates policy rules and modifies sensitive text strings in-place.
options.C: Define a postToolUse hook in a hooks.json file bound to the post-tool execution event, and implement an asynchronous handler function that cleans the modified file on disk after execution completes.
options.D: Define a Transform hook in a hooks.json file bound to the pre-tool execution event, and implement a handler function that mutates the payload parameter stream before returning it to the execution context.

question: A dedicated agent identity needs a financial-data bucket in a dedicated approved project. Bucket-scoped IAM already grants only its required operations, and all other storage buckets are in other projects. You need an additional resource-eligibility boundary so a later broad allow role cannot enable access to those other projects, for permissions supported by the chosen enforcement version. What should you do?
explanation: PABs restrict eligibility at supported Resource Manager scopes and do not grant access. Keep bucket IAM separate, verify supported permissions and account for the union of all applicable PABs. A project boundary does not distinguish buckets inside that project. ([PAB policies](https://docs.cloud.google.com/iam/docs/principal-access-boundary-policies))

options.A: Apply IAM Conditions to the agent identity’s IAM policy bindings, and restrict storage.objects.* permissions to resource names matching the designated financial bucket.
options.B: Configure a VPC Service Controls perimeter around the storage project, and define an ingress policy that permits Cloud Storage API operations only when invoked by the specific agent identity principal.
options.C: Bind a principal access boundary to the principal set containing the agent identity, allowing eligibility only for the approved project; retain the bucket-scoped IAM grant and ensure no other applicable PAB expands eligibility.
options.D: Configure an IAM Deny policy on the organization node to block all service accounts from accessing the storage buckets.

question: An enterprise financial agent sends supported tool payloads through Agent Gateway. You need to screen these payloads for sensitive-data leakage before forwarding and centralize request status/latency telemetry. Token usage is captured separately at the model layer with an agent correlation ID. Which TWO configuration steps should you take?
explanation: Use supported Model Armor screening and documented gateway logs; export logs through Cloud Logging sinks. Token accounting requires model-layer usage instrumentation and correlation, not an assumed route-level exporter. ([Gateway screening](https://docs.cloud.google.com/gemini-enterprise-agent-platform/govern/configure-model-armor))

options.A: Configure the Agent Gateway ingress route to disable TLS decryption.
options.B: Enable documented gateway request logging/tracing, and configure a Cloud Logging sink to BigQuery for centralized analysis; correlate separately instrumented model usage by agent identity.
options.C: Apply a supported Model Armor gateway template with Sensitive Data Protection inspection/de-identification settings and the required blocking/redaction enforcement mode.
options.D: Deploy an in-container eviction hook in the third-party partner API server to push telemetry metrics back to Agent Gateway.
options.E: Configure a VPC Service Controls perimeter around external third-party API private IP addresses to perform deep packet inspection and sanitization on egress HTTPS traffic.

question:
You are designing a multiagent system on Google Cloud in which multiple autonomous agents deployed in Agent Runtime collaborate through a graph workflow and pass context along sequential task routes. You want to ensure that each agent operates with least-privilege access and that its specific actions can be traced independently.

What should you do?
explanation: Agent Runtime can provision a unique agent identity for each deployment. Granting each identity only the IAM permissions needed for its target resources supports least privilege, while logs can identify the agent responsible for an action. Agent Registry supports discovery of agents and their endpoints for agent-to-agent communication. ([docs.cloud.google.com](https://docs.cloud.google.com/gemini-enterprise-agent-platform/scale/runtime/agent-identity))

options.A: Create a unique agent identity for each agent in Agent Runtime, register the agents in the Agent Registry, and grant the agent identity principal the necessary IAM roles for specific endpoints.
options.B: Use Agent Development Kit (ADK) local session state using the ToolContext parameter to dynamically store and propagate user authorization credentials in memory.
options.C: Configure a dedicated service account for each agent in Agent Runtime, grant least-privilege IAM roles to each service account for target resources, and use standard Cloud Audit Logs for auditability.
options.D: Store API keys in Secret Manager, and enable agents to retrieve keys to authorize communications.

question:
You are designing authentication controls for an Agent Development Kit (ADK) agent on Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform. The agent queries internal BigQuery datasets and will soon expand to call external third-party APIs. You want to enable secure, granular outbound tool authentication without managing custom credential vaults or hardcoding secrets in backend code.

What should you do?
explanation: An agent’s SPIFFE-based identity can be granted IAM permissions to access BigQuery using its own authority. Agent Identity auth manager securely stores third-party credentials and integrates with ADK to retrieve credentials and inject authentication headers, avoiding custom vault management and hardcoded secrets. ([docs.cloud.google.com](https://docs.cloud.google.com/iam/docs/auth-agent-own-identity))

options.A: Attach a service account to the ADK agent runtime for BigQuery access, and store third-party API keys in Secret Manager for backend code to retrieve during tool execution.
options.B: Enable Identity-Aware Proxy (IAP) on the Agent Platform host to secure BigQuery access, and configure OAuth 2.0 client IDs to broker outbound tokens for external APIs.
options.C: Assign IAM permissions for BigQuery to the agent’s Secure Production Identity Framework for Everyone (SPIFFE)-based agent identity, and store third-party credentials in Agent Identity auth manager to let ADK handle token retrieval and header injection.
options.D: Configure Cloud Key Management Service (Cloud KMS) to encrypt third-party API credentials in backend configuration files, and grant the Cloud KMS Decrypter IAM role to the agent’s compute service account.
